problem: Grace Poole comes and goes through the 'third-floor staircase door' and returns to her 'upper rooms', but the same paragraph then places her room 'on the second floor'. A reader tracking the house's geography (important later) is told two different floors.
new_text: The party was expected to arrive on Thursday afternoon, in time for dinner at six. During the wait, I had no time to nurse fantasies, and I believe I was as active and cheerful as anyone—except Adèle. Still, now and then, something dampened my spirits and threw me back, despite myself, into the territory of doubts, forebodings, and dark speculation. This happened when I chanced to see the third-floor staircase door (which lately had always been kept locked) open slowly and give passage to Grace Poole, in her neat cap, white apron, and handkerchief. I watched her glide along the gallery, her quiet step muffled in a cloth slipper; I saw her look into the busy, upside-down bedrooms, perhaps say a word to the charwoman about the proper way to polish a grate, clean a marble mantelpiece, or remove stains from wallpaper, and then move on. She would descend to the kitchen once a day, eat her dinner, smoke a moderate pipe by the hearth, and go back, carrying her pot of porter for her own private comfort to her gloomy upper rooms. Only one hour out of twenty-four did she spend with the other servants below; the rest of her time was spent in some low-ceilinged, oak-panelled room on the third floor. There she sat and sewed—and probably laughed bleakly to herself—as solitary as a prisoner in a dungeon.

problem: A full sentence of unexplained French; unlike Adèle's other French lines, nothing around it lets an English reader or listener grasp what she says (that at her mother's she followed the guests about and watched the maids dress the ladies). A short English echo keeps the French and restores meaning.
new_text: "Chez maman," she said, "quand il y avait du monde, je le suivais partout, au salon et à leurs chambres; souvent je regardais les femmes de chambre coiffer et habiller les dames, et c'était si amusant: comme cela on apprend." At Mama's, she explained, whenever there were guests she followed them everywhere, into the drawing room and their bedrooms, and watched the maids do the ladies' hair and dress them—it was such fun, and that was how you learned.

problem: 'of the kind the French call a cheeky little face' reads oddly (the French phrase has been dropped, so it sounds as if the French call it that in English). Simplify.
new_text: First, there was Mrs. Eshton and two of her daughters. She had clearly been a handsome woman and was well preserved still. Of her daughters, the eldest, Amy, was rather small—naive and childlike in face and manner, with a pretty figure. Her white muslin dress and blue sash suited her well. The second, Louisa, was taller and more elegant; with a very pretty, saucy little face. Both sisters were fair as lilies.

problem: 'the pious lady' is an ironic reference to Lady Ingram, but no one has been called pious; a listener cannot tell who is meant until the next paragraph's 'her ladyship'. Name her.
new_text: Mrs. Dent here leaned over to Lady Ingram and whispered something in her ear; I suppose, from the answer it drew, it was a reminder that a member of the hated tribe was present.

problem: The charade's answer 'Bridewell' (Bride + well) is an old name for a prison; most modern readers will not know this, so the joke and the prisoner scene do not click. A brief gloss.
new_text: "Bridewell!" exclaimed Colonel Dent—Bride, well, and the old name for a prison—and the charade was solved.

problem: 'as black as a crock' (a sooty cooking pot) is obscure dialect; readers will not get the image.
new_text: "A shockingly ugly old creature, miss; almost as black as a sooty pot."

problem: The speaker is called 'Mrs. Lynn', but throughout the batch she is 'Lady Lynn' (17.64, 17.75, 17.85, 18.32). A reader will think a new character has appeared.
new_text: "My dear boys, what are you thinking of?" exclaimed Lady Lynn.

problem: 'She has laid it carefully aside for you. I watched her do it.' — 'she' refers back to personified Chance two sentences earlier, across an intervening sentence about the gypsy herself; listeners may take 'she' as Miss Ingram (just discussed). Repeat the noun.
new_text: "Your fortune is still uncertain: when I studied your face, one trait contradicted another. Chance has set aside a measure of happiness for you—that I know. I knew it before I came here this evening. Chance has laid it carefully aside for you. I watched her do it. It depends on you to reach out your hand and take it. But whether you will—that is the question I am studying. Kneel again on the rug."
